turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Um, I came in because I'm just having a really hard time lately. I can't stop focusing on how the left side of my face looks. It just looks really uneven and puffy to me. 

I notice it constantly, especially on video calls for work—I'm a computer support specialist, so I'm on camera a lot—and in photos from my salsa classes. The frustrating part is that my friends and family keep telling me they don't see anything at all, but it's literally all I can see. It's gotten to the point where it's really starting to mess with my job and my social life, so I figured I needed to finally talk to someone about it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports being persistently preoccupied with perceived puffiness and asymmetry on the left side of their face that others explicitly do not observe.

turns.doctor_question: When you look in the mirror or on video, do you actually see the puffiness and unevenness that you're describing, or does it seem like the problem is more in how much you're thinking about your appearance even though others say it looks normal?
turns.patient_response:
I actually do see it. It doesn't feel like I'm just thinking about it too much. When I look at the screen during my work calls, or when I see those photos from my salsa class, the puffiness and unevenness on the left side is right there. It's clear as day to me. 

I know everyone else keeps telling me they don't see anything, which is really confusing, but to my eyes, it's incredibly obvious. And because I see it so clearly, I just can't stop focusing on it. It's constantly on my mind, and that's exactly why it's getting in the way of my job and making me want to avoid my social life.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with perceived facial puffiness and asymmetry that is obvious to them but unobservable to others, noting they cannot stop focusing on it.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a dermatologist or another doctor examine your face closely and tell you what they actually see regarding the puffiness and unevenness on the left side?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't. I mean, I go to my regular doctor for checkups, but I've never specifically asked them to look at my face or point it out to a dermatologist. I guess I've just been dealing with it on my own and trying to hide it. I haven't really wanted to draw professional attention to it, honestly, until it started getting this bad.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your face in mirrors, taking photos to examine it, or doing things like adjusting your hair or makeup to try to fix how the left side looks? And if so, do you feel like you have to do these things, even if you don't want to?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do that all the time. Um, especially right before my work meetings or if I'm getting ready to go out. I'll just keep opening the camera preview on my screen... and I'll sit there changing the angle, adjusting the lighting, and fixing my hair around that side of my face to try and hide it. 

I also end up taking and retaking a bunch of pictures on my phone just to check how it looks. And I'm constantly asking my friends if I look strange. I definitely feel like I have to do it, even when I really don't want to. I just can't stop myself. A lot of times I end up making myself late, or... honestly, I just get so drained from doing all that checking that I don't even want to go out anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes engaging in repetitive behaviors in response to appearance concerns, including repeatedly checking camera previews, taking photos, camouflaging with hair, and asking friends for reassurance.

turns.doctor_question: When you're checking your face or adjusting your hair and makeup, do you ever pick at your skin, squeeze, scratch, or otherwise damage the skin on your face, even if just a little bit?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't really do that. Um, I mean, I'll touch my face a lot to fix my hair or try to blend my makeup differently, but I don't pick at my skin or squeeze anything. It's not really an issue with my skin itself, it's just the shape and the puffiness. So, no, I'm not scratching or damaging it at all.

turns.doctor_question: If you brought a trusted friend or family member with you to see a dermatologist right now, do you think the doctor would be able to see and confirm the puffiness and unevenness on the left side of your face that you see, or do you think they would tell you they don't see anything wrong?
turns.patient_response:
I think... honestly, they would probably tell me they don't see anything. That's what everyone else says. My friends keep telling me they don't see anything wrong when I ask them. 

But I just can't stop focusing on it. I can clearly see how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks, especially on my video calls for work or in photos from my salsa classes. That's actually why I came in to see you. Even if other people say they don't notice it, I do, and it's just... it's starting to really mess with my work and my social life.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with a perceived facial asymmetry/puffiness that others and potential specialists cannot see, causing functional impairment in work and social life.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned that this focus on your face is affecting your work and social life. Can you tell me more specifically—like, how many days per week would you say this preoccupation is really interfering with what you need to get done, or causing you significant emotional distress?
turns.patient_response:
I'd say it's interfering almost every day, honestly. Um, at work, I've actually missed some important ticket deadlines, and I've joined a few video calls late just because I couldn't get past how I looked in the camera preview. It got to the point where my supervisor actually brought it up during my last performance review. 

And socially, it's definitely taking a toll. I've skipped out on my salsa nights and a few community events recently, especially when I knew people would be taking photos. I just couldn't handle the thought of being in them. So yeah, it's causing a lot of distress pretty much all week.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms experiencing severe daily preoccupation and distress regarding their appearance, noting they miss deadlines and avoid social events because they cannot bear being seen in photos or camera previews.

turns.doctor_question: I'd like to understand this better. Have you ever actually had a dermatologist or your primary care doctor examine your face and write down or tell you specifically what they found—whether they confirmed the puffiness and unevenness, or whether they said your face looks completely normal?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't actually done that. Um, I haven't been to a dermatologist about it, and I've never brought it up with my primary care doctor during a regular checkup either. So, no, I haven't had a medical professional examine my face or tell me officially what they see.

turns.doctor_question: When your friends and family tell you they don't see the puffiness and unevenness on your face, do you think they might actually be right and you could be mistaken about what you're seeing, or do you believe they're just not seeing it the way you do?
turns.patient_response:
Um... I guess part of me knows they could be right, just because literally everyone tells me the same thing. But... it's really hard to actually believe them. 

When I look in the mirror or at a photo, it's just so obvious to me. So I mostly end up thinking they just aren't looking closely enough, or... or maybe they're just trying to be nice so I don't feel bad about myself. Even if I try to tell myself I might be mistaken, my brain just goes right back to believing they just aren't seeing it the way I do.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes viewing a perceived facial defect that is obvious to them when looking in the mirror, despite acknowledging that others consistently do not see it.

turns.doctor_question: If you went to a dermatologist tomorrow and they examined your face very carefully and told you 'I don't see any puffiness or unevenness on the left side of your face—your face looks symmetric and normal'—would you be able to believe them, or would you still think they were missing something?
turns.patient_response: Honestly... I think I'd still struggle to believe them. Even if a professional looked really closely and told me everything was normal, I'd probably just think they missed it somehow. Or that maybe the lighting in their office was masking it. I want to be able to just accept it and move on, but... I don't think I could. I'd probably still leave there thinking they just didn't see what I see.
